concepts.query:
Content Discovery

Content discovery is a discovery practice that studies an existing content collection itself: inventorying and auditing what it holds, and working out what that content means, how it is structured and how well it serves its purpose.

We exported every page on the site into a spreadsheet and audited the collection: who owns each page, when it was last updated, what type of content it is and which topics it covers. Reading a sample closely showed what the content actually means, how it is structured and how well each section serves its purpose, before any redesign began.

Contextual Research

Contextual research is a discovery practice that studies the conditions surrounding a product or content collection rather than the content or its users: the business, organizational, technical and market circumstances in which it exists.

Before redesigning the portal, we studied the conditions around it rather than the content itself: the organization's reporting lines, its procurement rules, the technical limits of the platform it runs on and the market of competing services. That contextual research explained why earlier redesigns had stalled and which constraints any new structure had to respect.

Competitive Review

Competitive review is a contextual research method that assesses competitors' products, sites or services against criteria that matter to the organization commissioning it, showing where that organization stands and what its audiences already expect.

For the credit union's redesign, we reviewed six competitors' websites against criteria that mattered to the organization: how clearly each explained fees, how easily members could find rates and how each handled online applications. The competitive review showed where the credit union stood and what its members had come to expect from similar services.

Heuristic Analysis

Heuristic analysis is a discovery method in which an expert reviews an existing site or product against established usability and user experience heuristics, identifying where it follows or departs from them without testing it with users.

Without recruiting any participants, I reviewed the existing checkout flow against established usability heuristics: visibility of system status, consistency, error prevention, and recognition rather than recall. The heuristic analysis noted where the site followed or departed from each one, rated each problem's severity and gave the team a ranked list to fix before testing with users.

Process Mapping

Process mapping is a contextual research method that documents and diagrams the business processes surrounding a product or content collection, particularly handoffs between systems and people, to expose inefficiencies and unintended consequences in how work actually gets done.

We followed a grant application from submission to payment, documenting every step, system and handoff. The process map showed applications waiting days in a shared inbox, data rekeyed between two systems and a review step nobody owned. Diagramming the business process exposed those inefficiencies, and showed where better content and tools would actually help.

Stakeholder Engagement

Stakeholder engagement is a project management practice of identifying the people and groups with an interest in a project, learning what they need from it and what they can contribute, and keeping them informed and involved in its decisions throughout, so that their knowledge shapes the work and their concerns are addressed before they become obstacles.

We started by identifying everyone with an interest in the redesign and asking what they needed from it and what they could contribute. Throughout the project we kept those stakeholders informed and involved in decisions, shared work in progress for critique, and addressed concerns early, before a disagreement about the navigation could become an obstacle.

User Research

User research is a discovery practice that studies the people a product or content collection serves, learning their behaviors, needs and motivations directly from them through observation, conversation and task-based methods.

To understand the people the archive serves, we spent time with researchers, students and staff, observing how they look for records, asking about their goals and frustrations, and watching them complete real tasks. That user research revealed needs and motivations no analytics dashboard showed, including how often people search for a person rather than a document.

Contextual Inquiry

Contextual inquiry is a user research technique used to understand behavior by either observing users in their real world environments, or staging scenarios to mimic those environments. Contextual inquiry uses direct observation to help to counter the recall and reporting bias that asking users about behavior can entail. 

Rather than asking warehouse staff how they used the inventory system, we observed them at work during a busy shift, watching where they looked things up and what notes they kept beside the screen. Direct observation in their real environment surfaced workarounds nobody had mentioned in interviews, and countered the recall bias that self-reported behavior carries.

Mental Models

A mental model is a human factors concept that describes a user's conceptual understanding of a service, product, topic, or set of content. Mental models can be elicited by single research techniques (such as card sorting) or synthesized from mixed methods. Mental models may be captured as narratives (for example with personas), a set of findings, or a graphical model such as a flow diagram.

In interviews, riders described the transit pass as money stored on a card, not a ticket for a set number of rides, so they expected to top it up rather than renew it. We synthesized that mental model across sessions and support requests and wrote it up as a short narrative: what people believed the service was, how they thought it worked and what they expected next. The site's ticket products contradicted it at every step.

User Interviews

User interviews are a user research method of focused one-to-one or small-group conversations that elicit how people think about a subject, along with their preferences and their behavior as they recall it. Interviews may include interactive tasks.

We held twelve one-to-one interviews with small business owners, asking how they think about payroll, which tools they prefer and how they handled their last tax filing, as they recall it. Each interview ended with a short interactive task on the current site. The conversations surfaced vocabulary and priorities we later used to label the new sections.

Best Practices

Best practices are a design approach of building on methods and conventions proven across many projects and contexts, and judging work against them, rather than solving each problem from first principles.

Rather than invent a navigation pattern for the new intranet, we started from conventions proven across many sites: a persistent global menu, breadcrumbs and a predictable footer. We reviewed the established guidance for forms and labels, judged our early designs against it, and departed from a best practice only where research showed our users' situation was genuinely different.

Collaborative Design

Collaborative design is a design approach in which the people with a stake in a solution, including clients, subject experts, users and the teams who will build and maintain it, take part in designing it, so that decisions draw on their combined knowledge and earn their shared commitment.

The new patient portal was designed in collaborative working sessions with clinicians, schedulers, patients and the developers who would build it. Each group sketched, critiqued and chose between options together, so decisions drew on their combined knowledge. Because everyone had a hand in shaping the design, the team shared a commitment to it long after the workshops ended.

Design Principles

The formulation of design principles is a design approach in which a team states the fundamental rules a design must follow, specific to its problem, organization and audience, and uses them to make, explain and evaluate decisions consistently throughout the work.

Before sketching, the team agreed on five design principles specific to the library's audience, such as "plain words over catalog terms" and "every page says what to do next." When two options competed, we tested each against the principles, which kept our decisions consistent and easy to explain, and gave us criteria for evaluating the finished design.

Systems Thinking

Systems thinking is a design approach that treats a product, content collection or organization as a system of interacting parts, people and processes, attending to how they influence one another over time, including the delayed and nonlinear effects that make outcomes hard to predict.

A category added for one campaign quietly broke navigation another team relied on, and the cleanup came months later. A systems thinking approach treats the site, its content and the people who maintain it as one system of interacting parts and processes, watching how changes influence each other over time, including the delayed and nonlinear effects no single team would predict.

Semantic Web

The semantic web is an engineering practice of making the meaning of data explicit, describing things and their relationships with shared, formally defined vocabularies so that software can integrate and reason over data from many sources. It spans the open web of data and the semantic layers organizations build over their own systems.

"Semantic web" refers to the web of "machine readable information," as opposed to the web of "pages." Semantic web applications are often built on technologies that support the encoding and inference of "meaning," including RDF, RDFS, and OWL. 

We published the museum's collection with its meaning made explicit: each artwork, artist and place has a URI and is described with shared, formally defined vocabularies. Other institutions' data can now be integrated with ours, software can reason over the combined graph to infer connections no single catalog records, and the same ontology forms a semantic layer over internal systems.

Knowledge Graphs

A knowledge graph is an engineering outcome in which the entities of a domain and the typed relationships between them are represented as connected data that software can query and reason over, inferring facts that were never stated directly and integrating information from many sources.

For a food bank, we modeled distribution sites, neighborhoods and services as entities with typed relationships: a site serves a neighborhood and offers fresh produce. Integrating schedules from several sources into one knowledge graph, software can query the connected data and infer answers no source states directly, such as which nearby sites are open today.

Linked Data

Linked data is an engineering outcome in which the things a site or service describes are also published as structured statements that software can interpret, using shared vocabularies such as schema.org and identifiers that link to other data. On the web it is most often embedded in pages as JSON-LD.

Each event page on the site now includes JSON-LD describing the event with schema.org: its name, dates, venue, performers and ticket offers, with links to the venue's and performers' own identifiers. Search engines read that linked data to show event details directly in results, and partner calendars import it without anyone copying listings by hand.

Information Architecture

Information Architecture is the structural design of shared information spaces. Information architecture methods focus on organizing, structuring, and labeling content in an effective and sustainable way in order to help users find information and complete tasks.

When people can't find information on a site, the cause is usually structural. Information architecture work organizes, structures and labels the content of a shared information space: how it is classified, what each category is called and how people move through it. Each part is designed and tested so users can find what they need and complete their tasks, and the structure holds as content grows.

Navigation Design

Navigation design is a user experience design practice that shapes how people move through a site or product: the navigation model, and the menus, links and signposts that show people where they are, where they can go and how to get there.

We redesigned how people move through the university site. A simpler navigation model puts five audience-based entry points in the main menu, breadcrumbs show where people are, and contextual links on each page point to where they can go next. Secondary navigation allows them to move easily within explicitly defined sections. Clear signposts at every level mean a visitor arriving from a search engine can still find their way around.

Search

Search is an information architecture practice concerned with a site's search system itself: how its index is built, how queries are parsed and results ranked for relevance, and how the results page, filters, autocomplete and synonyms help people retrieve a known item or refine an exploratory query.

Applies to writing about designing, configuring or tuning search: indexing, relevance ranking, query handling, search results interfaces and search log analysis.

The search logs showed which queries returned zero results. We added synonyms so abbreviations and old product names match current terms, tuned relevance ranking so title and topic matches outrank body text, and rebuilt the results page with filters and autocomplete. Known-item searches now land on the first page of results, and exploratory searches can be refined instead of abandoned.

Taxonomy

Taxonomy is an information architecture practice concerned with controlled vocabularies: the named, usually hierarchical sets of concepts an organization uses to classify content consistently, so that it can be retrieved, filtered and related through them. It spans a vocabulary's whole life, from designing it, to putting it to work in systems, to keeping it effective over time.

Includes taxonomy development, governance and implementation: designing a vocabulary, keeping it effective once it is in use, and putting it to work in systems, including migration between platforms and integration with them.

We turned a drifting tag list into a controlled vocabulary: a preferred label, alternate labels and a definition for each concept, arranged in a shallow hierarchy so editors classify content consistently. Stored as a standards compliant SKOS taxonomy, each tag references a managed concept that drives filters, retrieval and related content, and a regular review keeps the taxonomy effective as new subjects appear.

User Experience Design

User experience design is a design practice that shapes the whole of a person's experience with an organization, its services and its products, using research to coordinate content, tools and interactions across that experience rather than designing any one of them in isolation.

We designed the whole experience of renewing a professional license, not just the form: the reminder email, the explanation of requirements, the payment step and the confirmation that follows. Research with license holders guided how content, tools and interactions were coordinated across each stage, so the renewal felt like one service rather than a string of separate pages.

Interaction Design

Interaction design is a user experience design practice that specifies how a product responds to what people do: the actions available to them, the feedback they receive and the states an interface moves through, designed so that responses are predictable and coherent.

We specified how the booking form responds to every action: which choices become available after a date is picked, what feedback appears when a time slot is full, and how the interface moves between its loading, error and confirmation states. Each response was designed to be predictable and coherent, so people always knew what had happened and what to do next.

Automation

Automation is an engineering practice of handing repeatable tasks to software, so that they run on a trigger or a schedule with little or no human intervention. In content work it covers rule-based and model-driven handling of tasks such as tagging, transforming, validating and publishing content, wherever volume or consistency makes manual work impractical.

Tagging two thousand legacy articles by hand wasn't practical, so we automated it: a script runs each night, classifies new and changed articles against the vocabulary, validates required fields and flags anything below a confidence threshold for an editor. The repeatable work now runs on a schedule with little human intervention, and people handle only the exceptions.

Python

Python is a general-purpose programming language, most often run on servers and from the command line, and widely used for data analysis, natural language processing and machine learning. It is valued for code that is easy to read and write, a large ecosystem of libraries and a large, supportive community.

I wrote a Python script to analyze the article archive: it loads every document, uses an NLP library to extract keywords and entities, and writes the results to a CSV for review. Python's readable syntax and large ecosystem of libraries made the analysis quick to build, and the script runs from the command line whenever the archive changes.

Javascript

JavaScript is a programming language and, alongside HTML and CSS, a core technology of the web. Browsers run it to make pages interactive, from light, progressively enhanced features to frameworks such as React that render entire sites as single-page applications, and it also runs on servers through runtimes such as Node.js.

The product page works without JavaScript, then progressively enhances: a small script adds an image zoom and live stock updates in the browser. The account area is a React single-page application, and the same JavaScript validation code runs on the server under Node.js, so each form rule is written once and enforced in both places.

Technology Integration

Technology integration is an engineering practice of fitting new tools and services into an organization's existing systems, content and workflows, connecting them so that they exchange data and work as part of one process rather than as separate products. It covers the interfaces, configuration and changes to working practice that adoption requires.

Includes integrating AI models and services into content and publishing workflows.

The newsroom adopted a language model to draft summaries, but only after integrating it into the existing publishing workflow: the CMS sends each new article to the service, stores the draft summary in its own field and routes it to an editor for review. Connected this way, the tool exchanges data with existing systems instead of becoming one more product to manage.

Evaluation

Evaluation is a design practice that assesses whether a proposed or existing solution achieves what it was designed to achieve, by testing it with people, inspecting it against criteria or measuring how it performs.

Once the new structure was built, we evaluated whether it achieved what it was designed to do. We tested key tasks with people, inspected pages against accessibility and content criteria, and measured how long pages took to load and how often searches succeeded. The results showed which goals the design met and where it needed another round of work.

Performance Evaluation

Performance evaluation is an evaluation method that assesses how quickly and efficiently a website or application delivers its content and functionality, including over slow connections and on less capable devices, and whether it makes people download more than their experience requires.

We measured how quickly the news site delivered content on a mid-range phone over a slow connection. The performance evaluation found nearly three megabytes of scripts and images on the home page, much of it never used, and a web font that blocked rendering. After trimming the payload, the first article loaded in under two seconds, even on less capable devices.

Usability Testing

Usability testing is an evaluation method in which representative users attempt realistic tasks with a product, prototype or body of content while researchers observe where they succeed, struggle or fail, in order to find and fix problems in its design.

Includes design prototype testing.

Five representative users attempted realistic tasks with a clickable prototype while we observed and they thought aloud. We noted where each one succeeded, struggled or failed: labels they misread, paths they abandoned, answers they didn't recognize. The team fixed the biggest design problems and tested the revised prototype again with a new round of participants.

Accessibility Evaluation

Accessibility evaluation is an evaluation method that assesses whether people with disabilities can use a website or application, including people who rely on assistive technologies such as screen readers and keyboard navigation, and people with conditions such as low vision or motion sensitivity.

We assessed whether people using assistive technologies could use the registration site: navigating every form by keyboard alone, listening to each page with a screen reader, checking color contrast for low vision and testing reduced-motion settings. The accessibility evaluation found unlabeled form fields and a focus trap in the date picker, and checked each fix against WCAG.

Content Modeling

Content modeling is an information architecture practice that defines the types of content an organization manages, the attributes each type is made of and the relationships between types, so that content can be managed as structured data and delivered across channels and platforms.

For a museum, we modeled exhibitions, artworks, artists and events as separate content types. Each type has its own attributes, such as an artwork's medium and year, and the relationships between types (an artist made an artwork, an exhibition includes it) link one page to the next. Managed as structured data in the CMS, the content model lets the same content be delivered to the website, a kiosk and partner channels.

Content Strategy

Content strategy is a design practice that plans for the creation, publication and governance of content to meet established goals: deciding what content an organization needs, for whom and in what form, and how it will be produced and sustained over time.

The college had thousands of pages and no plan. Our content strategy started from established goals for enrollment and student support, then decided what content each audience needed, in what form and from which team. We set a publishing plan, assigned owners and defined the governance that keeps content accurate, so the site could be sustained after relaunch.

Prototyping

Prototyping is building partial, provisional versions of a product, interface, content model or system in order to learn from them before committing to full production. As a design approach, it treats making as a way of thinking, testing ideas by building something people can try, react to and critique. As an engineering practice, it produces working code or configured software that proves a solution is feasible and exposes its constraints early.

Covers prototypes at every fidelity, from paper sketches and clickable mockups to coded prototypes built in the medium of the finished product.

We built a working prototype of the new knowledge base into the platform within two weeks: a few real content types, a hundred migrated articles and a rough front end. Testing it with staff showed which parts of the content model held up, and building it exposed a constraint in the platform's search that no diagram would have revealed before full production.

Sanity

Sanity is a content management system whose content lives in a hosted, real-time datastore, the Content Lake, is queried with GROQ, and is edited in Sanity Studio, an open-source React application that teams configure in code with schema types, desk structure, custom inputs, document actions and plugins.

Applies to writing about working with Sanity itself: configuring or extending Sanity Studio, defining schemas, writing GROQ queries, building with Sanity's plugins, functions and APIs, and Sanity's own events and builder community.

In Sanity Studio I defined schema types for articles and authors, customized the desk structure, added a custom input and a document action that checks required fields, and installed several plugins built by the Sanity community. A GROQ query pulls each article with its author and topics from the Content Lake, and a webhook rebuilds the site whenever an editor publishes.

Card Sorting

Card sorting is a user research method in which participants group cards labeled with content items or terms into categories that make sense to them, revealing how they expect information to be grouped and labeled.

Thirty participants sorted cards labeled with the site's main topics into groups that made sense to them, then named each group. The card sort revealed how people expect the information to be grouped and labeled: most put billing and payments together, and almost nobody used the internal term the organization had built its navigation around.

Tree Testing

Tree testing is an evaluation method in which participants look for given items in a text-only hierarchy of labels, testing whether a proposed structure and its labels match where people expect to find information.

Before building the new navigation, we ran a tree test: participants saw only a text hierarchy of labels and were asked where they would look for items like "replace a lost card" and "update an address." Success rates and the paths people took showed which labels matched their expectations and which parts of the proposed structure sent them the wrong way.

Domain Modeling

Domain modeling is a contextual research method that produces a structured representation of the key concepts in a subject area and the salient relationships between them, so that later structural design rests on how the domain itself is organized.

Working with subject matter experts, we mapped the key concepts in a city's permitting domain (permits, projects, properties, inspections and the people involved) and the relationships between them. That domain model gave us a structured representation of how the subject itself is organized, so the later content model and navigation could rest on it rather than on the org chart.

User Interface Design

User interface design is a design practice concerned with the visible, operable surface of a product: the layout, typography, color, controls and visual hierarchy through which people perceive content and act on it, and the way that surface adapts across screen sizes and devices.

Includes visual design, responsive layout and systems of reusable interface components.

We redesigned the dashboard's visual hierarchy so the most important figures stand out: a clear typographic scale, restrained color, consistent controls and generous spacing. The layout adapts from a wide desktop grid to a single column on phones, and every element comes from a shared library of interface components, so the visible surface stays consistent across screens.

Site Maps

A site map is an information architecture model of a website's structure: its pages or page types and the hierarchical and navigational relationships among them. Usually drawn as an organization-chart style diagram, it is used to plan, communicate and review a site's structure with a team.

Covers site maps as design artifacts, including their limits for large, changing content collections and the alternatives that model the same structure.

The site map for the redesign showed every page type and section as boxes in a hierarchy, with lines for the main navigational paths between them. We used the diagram to plan the structure with the team and review it with stakeholders, while noting its limit: for a collection that grows weekly, it shows where pages sit, not the rules that decide where new ones go.

Content Operations

Content operations is a content strategy practice concerned with running content as an ongoing function: the people, workflows, tools and policies through which an organization produces, reviews, maintains and retires content at scale, and keeps the structures that support it current as needs change.

Includes governance: the decision rights, rules and maintenance routines that keep content, models and vocabularies effective over time.

To run content as an ongoing function rather than a launch project, the team mapped the workflows by which articles are produced, reviewed, published and retired, named an owner for each step and set policies for review dates. We also designed the team's technology solution to work with their content operation, as opposed to against it. Governance meetings now approve changes to the content model and the vocabulary, so the structures behind the content stay current at scale.

Web Writing

Web writing is a content strategy practice concerned with the words themselves: writing and editing for how people read on screens, where they scan, search and arrive in the middle of a journey, with language that is clear, concise and consistent across a site.

Includes editorial style guides and the voice, tone and terminology guidance that keeps a team's writing consistent.

We rewrote the service pages for how people read on screens: they scan, search and often arrive in the middle of a task. Headings now state what each section answers, sentences are short, and one term is used consistently for each idea. A brief style guide set the voice, tone and terminology so every writer on the team produces clear, concise copy.

Discovery

Discovery is the design practice of learning what can be known about a product or content collection before and while changing it: what it holds, who uses it and why, the conditions it operates in, and what it costs and returns to build and maintain.

Before proposing changes to the agency's site, we spent three weeks in discovery: inventorying what the site holds, interviewing the people who use it and why, reviewing the systems and budget it depends on, and learning what it costs to maintain. That understanding of the product and the conditions around it shaped every recommendation that followed.

Structural Analysis

Structural analysis is both a content discovery and an evaluation method: the systematic assessment of how a content collection is built, including its content types, the attributes they are composed of and the relationships between elements in a given implementation, in order to keep what works and improve what does not.

We assessed how the product catalog was built: the content types in the CMS, the attributes each one is composed of and the relationships linking products, parts and manuals. The structural analysis found fields used inconsistently, relationships stored as plain text and types that duplicated each other, so the new model could keep what worked and fix what didn't.

Human Centered Design

Human-centered design is a design approach that grounds every decision in the needs, abilities, goals and contexts of the people who will use what is being designed. It involves those people throughout the work, through research and iterative evaluation, rather than starting from the technology or the organization's structure.

Includes user-centered design, and the human-centered design process codified in ISO 9241-210.

We grounded every decision for the benefits application in the needs, abilities and contexts of the people applying: many on phones, some using screen readers, most short on time. They took part throughout, through interviews, early prototypes and repeated rounds of evaluation, so the design followed their goals rather than the agency's internal structure.

Goals

Goals are project management assets that capture the objectives a project exists to achieve, whether for the business, its users or the organization, together with the work of defining, prioritizing and agreeing on them. Agreed upon goals give scope, design decisions and measures of success something to be traced back to.

Includes success criteria and the measures used to tell whether a goal has been met.

At the kickoff we worked with leadership to define three goals for the redesign: raise online applications by a fifth, cut calls about application status in half and make every service page accessible. Each goal had a measure and a target. When later requests competed for time, we traced each one back to those agreed goals to decide what made the scope.

Use Cases

Use cases is a project management assets that describe the specific situations in which people or systems will use what is being built, covering who is acting, what they are trying to accomplish and in what circumstances. Identifying and documenting them grounds requirements, scope and priorities in concrete needs rather than in features.

Includes user stories, scenarios and the requirements derived from them.

Before writing requirements, we documented the use cases the new portal had to support: a parent registering a child for school, a teacher updating a class roster, an administrator exporting attendance. Each described who was acting, what they were trying to accomplish and in what circumstances, so scope and priorities rested on concrete needs rather than a feature list.

Natural Language Processing

Natural language processing is an engineering practice that uses computational methods to analyze, interpret or generate human language, turning unstructured text into data that software can work with. Typical tasks include extracting keywords and entities, classifying and clustering documents, and measuring how similar two texts are.

Includes statistical and machine learning techniques applied to text, from term frequency analysis to embeddings and semantic similarity. Concerns the techniques; the models and services that apply them are engineering tools.

To find recurring themes in five years of support tickets, we used natural language processing: the text was cleaned and tokenized, keywords and named entities were extracted, and tickets were clustered by similarity using embeddings. Turning that unstructured text into data showed which problems came up most, and which tickets described the same issue in different words.

Standards Compliance

Standards compliance is an engineering practice of building systems, content and data to conform to published, consensus-based specifications, such as those for markup, accessibility, metadata and vocabularies. Working to a shared standard lets the results behave predictably across browsers, platforms and organizations, and keeps them usable as tools change.

Includes adopting a standard deliberately as the basis for a design or implementation, as well as testing conformance to it.

We rebuilt the site to conform to published standards: valid, semantic HTML, WCAG accessibility criteria, schema.org metadata and a SKOS vocabulary for topics. Validators run on every build to test conformance. Working to shared specifications means the site behaves predictably across browsers and assistive technologies, and its data stays usable as the tools around it change.

Programming Languages

A programming language is an engineering tool used to write operational code: a formal notation, with its own syntax and rules, for expressing programs or queries that a computer can execute. Languages differ in what they are designed for, from general-purpose programming to querying a particular kind of data.

The project used three programming languages, each for what it does best: JavaScript for the interactive front end, Python for the scripts that clean and analyze content data, and SPARQL for querying the knowledge graph. Each has its own syntax and rules for expressing what a computer should do, and choosing the right one for each task kept the code simple.

SPARQL

SPARQL is a query language, standardized by the W3C, for retrieving and updating data stored as RDF. Its queries match patterns of subject–relationship–object statements, so they can follow chains of relationships through a graph and combine data published at separate endpoints.

A SPARQL query against the museum's triple store finds every artwork by artists born in a given city, following relationships from artwork to artist to birthplace across the graph. A second query pulls in data from a public endpoint and combines both sources in one result, and an update query corrects a mistyped date across hundreds of records at once.

Engineering Products

An engineering product is an engineering tool delivered as a ready-made application, platform or service that a team adopts and configures rather than writes: the systems that store, manage, process and deliver content and data.

Rather than build a content repository, a search service and a deployment pipeline from scratch, the team adopted ready-made products for each and spent its time configuring them: content types in the CMS, an index in the hosted search service and build settings on the deployment platform. The engineering effort went into connecting those systems, not writing them.

CMS

A content management system is a product for creating, storing, organizing and publishing content, pairing an editing interface for authors with a content repository and a means of delivering content to websites and other channels. A headless CMS separates the repository from presentation and delivers structured content through an API to any number of front ends.

The team moved its content into a headless CMS: authors work in an editing interface with structured fields, the content repository stores each item once, and an API delivers it to the website, the mobile app and the digital signage. Separating content from presentation means a new channel can be added without changing how authors create and organize content.

Continuous Integration

Continuous integration is an engineering practice employed to automatically build, test and deploy software whenever changes are committed to a shared code repository, running defined workflows in a clean environment so that problems surface early and every release follows the same repeatable steps.

Includes continuous deployment, and workflows that rebuild and publish a site when its content changes.

Every commit to the site's repository triggers a workflow that installs dependencies, builds the site, runs link and accessibility checks, and deploys only if every check passes. The same workflow runs when an editor publishes in the CMS, so content changes go through identical, repeatable steps, and a broken build surfaces within minutes instead of in production.

AI

AI is a class of products that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as generating and summarizing text, answering questions and classifying information, using models trained on large amounts of data. It is most often encountered as large language models offered through assistants, services and programming interfaces.

Covers AI models and the assistants and services built on them: what they are, how they behave, and their strengths and limits in practice.

We tested how well a large language model could summarize policy documents and answer staff questions about them. The assistant produced fluent summaries and handled common questions well, but invented details when a document was ambiguous and struggled to classify edge cases. We kept it for drafting, with an editor checking every answer, and documented its limits for the team.

Graph Databases

A graph database is a product that stores data as nodes and the relationships between them, rather than as rows in tables, so that connected data can be queried by following relationships directly. Its structure can grow incrementally, adding new kinds of things and relationships without reorganizing what is already stored.

Includes both triple stores and labeled property graph databases.

We moved the parts catalog's relationships into a graph database: parts, assemblies, suppliers and documents are nodes, and the connections between them are stored directly as relationships. Queries that took several joins in the relational database now follow those relationships in one step, and new kinds of things can be added without reorganizing the data already stored.

Frameworks

A framework is an engineering tool that supplies a reusable structure of conventions, components and rules within which something is built, so that work starts from an established foundation rather than from scratch. Software frameworks structure how applications and websites are built; data frameworks structure how information is described and exchanged.

Starting the new site from a framework rather than from scratch gave us routing, a component model, a build pipeline and conventions for organizing files on the first day. The team spent its time on content and design instead of rebuilding that foundation, and new developers could find their way around because the framework's structure was already familiar.

RDF

RDF is a data framework, standardized by the W3C, for describing information as statements, each linking a subject to an object through a named relationship. Because things and relationships are identified by URIs, statements from different sources can be merged into a single graph and queried together.

Includes RDF serializations such as Turtle, and the languages layered on RDF for schemas, ontologies and validation, such as RDFS, OWL and SHACL.

We expressed the manufacturer's product data in RDF: every product, component and supplier has a URI, and each fact is a statement linking a subject to an object through a named relationship. Serialized as Turtle and validated with SHACL shapes, the statements merged cleanly with a partner's data into a single graph that both teams could query together.

Astro

Astro is a JavaScript framework for building content-driven websites. It renders pages to static HTML at build time by default, ships client-side JavaScript only for the components that need interactivity, and can draw content from a headless content management system or run as a server for pages rendered on request.

We rebuilt the marketing site in Astro: pages render to static HTML at build time from content in a headless CMS, and only the search box and an image carousel ship client-side JavaScript, as interactive islands. A few preview routes run on the server so editors can see drafts on request. Pages load fast because almost nothing runs in the browser.

Design Outcomes

A design outcome is an outcome that shows up in how well a product serves its intended audience: a quality of a content collection or information space, achieved through decisions about structure, interactions, labeling and relationships, and judged by how readily its audiences can find, understand and use what it holds.

Six months after the redesign, we judged it by how well the site served its audience: whether visitors could find the right service, understand what it required and complete it without calling the help desk. Those design outcomes, measured through task success and support volume, came from decisions about structure, labeling, interactions and the relationships between pages.

Interoperability

Interoperability is an engineering outcome that ensures content and data can be accessed and used by connected systems, services, and agents. Part of the FAIR data recommendation (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable).

The state's health departments each kept facility data in different systems. By agreeing on a shared schema and exchanging records through a common API, each department's data can now be accessed and used by the others' systems and by public services, without manual reformatting. Interoperable data made a statewide facility finder possible, and keeps it current.

Content Reuse

Content reuse is a design outcome in which content is created once and used in more than one place, channel or context, published as is or repurposed, rather than being rewritten or duplicated for each.

Each medication's safety warning is written once and stored as its own piece of content. The same warning appears on the drug's page, in the printable patient handout, in the mobile app and in a partner's formulary, published as is or shortened for small screens. When the warning changes, every channel updates without anyone rewriting or duplicating it.

Discoverability

Discoverability is a design outcome in which content, and the concepts, facts and ideas it holds, can be found and understood by the audiences it is intended for. It depends on how content is organized, labeled and connected, and on how well that matches what those audiences already know and expect.

Visitors couldn't find the foundation's research reports, even though they were on the site. We improved discoverability by organizing the reports by topic and audience, labeling them with the terms people actually use and connecting each report to related programs and news. People now find and understand what the reports offer, because the structure matches what they expect.

Engineering Outcomes

An engineering outcome is an outcome that shows up in systems and data themselves: a property of how content and data are encoded, stored and exchanged, achieved through implementation choices about formats, schemas and infrastructure, and judged by what software, services and agents can do with the result.

We judged the migration by what software could do with the result: content stored in an open format, every item with a stable identifier, data exchanged through a documented API and a schema that downstream systems could validate against. Those engineering outcomes came from implementation choices about formats, schemas and infrastructure, not from anything visible on the page.

Machine Readability

Machine readability is an engineering outcome in which content and data are encoded so that software can interpret their meaning, not merely display them: entities, facts and relationships are explicitly typed and structured, so that search engines, voice assistants, AI agents and other systems can retrieve, combine and act on them without human interpretation.

Covers the quality and the case for pursuing it, in content and markup as well as in data.

We made the clinic's opening hours, services and locations machine readable: each is entered as typed, structured data instead of a paragraph of prose, and published with explicit markup. Search engines, voice assistants and booking agents can now interpret and act on that information directly, answering "which clinic is open now" without a person reading the page.

Structured Content

Structured content is a design outcome in which organized, predictable, and consistent content that can be easily reused, repurposed, and understood by both humans and machines across various platforms and contexts. It is often marked up using specific languages to enhance usability and accessibility, and it is broken down into discrete, meaningful pieces for optimal management, interpretation, and display.

Rather than writing finished pages, the team broke each procedure into discrete, meaningful pieces: its steps, warnings, the device it applies to and its audience. That structured content is consistent and predictable enough for both people and machines to understand, so the same pieces are reused across the website, an app and a printed guide, and an update made once appears on every platform.

Cognition

Cognition is the human factors concept for mental processes that deal with knowledge. It includes psychological activities that acquire, store, retrieve, transform, or apply information.

Customers kept misreading the bank's new fee notice. The cognition involved explained why: most reading is fast and automatic, so people perceived familiar word shapes, interpreted new terms through what they already knew, and held little in memory past the first lines. Few slowed down to reason it through. The revision led with the key fact and built on existing knowledge, so it was easier to take in, recall and act on.

Decision Making

Decision making is the human factors study of how individuals make choices based on available information, habits, effort, and previous decisions. It is concerned with how and when decisions are rational and based on an individuals understood interests, and where they appear irrational or potentially counterproductive. 

Most new staff kept the minimum pension contribution they were enrolled at, even though the employer would have matched more. Their decision making explained it: comparing rates took effort, the default asked for nothing, and habit made the earlier choice feel safer than new information. We showed each person what a higher rate would add by retirement, so the rational choice became the easy one and nobody lost the freedom to choose.
